L15@P0: 1 Introduction
L16@P0: Imitation learning allows for control policies to be learned directly from example demonstrations
L17@P0: provided by human experts. It is easy to implement, and reduces or removes the need for extensive
L18@P0: interaction with the environment during training [58, 41, 4, 1, 20].
L19@P0: However, imitation learning suffers from a fundamental problem: distributional shift [9, 42]. Training
L20@P0: and testing state distributions are different, induced respectively by the expert and learned policies.
L21@P0: Therefore, imitating expert actions on expert trajectories may not align with the true task objective.
L22@P0: While this problem is widely acknowledged [41, 9, 42, 43], yet with careful engineering, naïve
L23@P0: behavioral cloning approaches have yielded good results for several practical problems [58, 41, 44,
L24@P0: 36, 37, 4, 33, 3]. This raises the question: is distributional shift really still a problem?
L25@P0: In this paper, we identify a somewhat surprising and very problematic effect of distributional shift:
L26@P0: “causal misidentification.” Distinguishing correlates of expert actions in the demonstration set from
L27@P0: true causes is usually very difficult, but may be ignored without adverse effects when training and
L28@P0: testing distributions are identical (as assumed in supervised learning), since nuisance correlates
L29@P0: continue to hold in the test set. However, this can cause catastrophic problems in imitation learning
L30@P0: due to distributional shift. This is exacerbated by the causal structure of sequential action: the very
L31@P0: fact that current actions cause future observations often introduces complex new nuisance correlates.
L32@P0: To illustrate, consider behavioral cloning to train a neural network to drive a car. In scenario A, the
L33@P0: model’s input is an image of the dashboard and windshield, and in scenario B, the input to the model
L34@P0: (with identical architecture) is the same image but with the dashboard masked out (see Fig 1). Both
L35@P0: cloned policies achieve low training loss, but when tested on the road, model B drives well, while
L36@P0: model A does not. The reason: the dashboard has an indicator light that comes on immediately when
L37@P0: the brake is applied, and model A wrongly learns to apply the brake only when the brake light is on.
L38@P0: Even though the brake light is the effect of braking, model A could achieve low training error by
L39@P0: misidentifying it as the cause instead.

L44@P1: relies on the braking indicator to decide whether to brake. Model B instead correctly attends to the pedestrian.
L45@P1: This situation presents a give-away symptom of causal misidentification: access to more information
L46@P1: leads to worse generalization performance in the presence of distributional shift. Causal misidentification occurs commonly in natural imitation learning settings, especially when the imitator’s inputs
L47@P1: include history information.
L48@P1: In this paper, we first point out and investigate the causal misidentification problem in imitation
L49@P1: learning. Then, we propose a solution to overcome it by learning the correct causal model, even when
L50@P1: using complex deep neural network policies. We learn a mapping from causal graphs to policies,
L51@P1: and then use targeted interventions to efficiently search for the correct policy, either by querying an
L52@P1: expert, or by executing selected policies in the environment.
L53@P1: 2 Related Work
L54@P1: Imitation learning. Imitation learning through behavioral cloning dates back to Widrow and Smith,
L55@P1: 1964 [58], and has remained popular through today [41, 44, 36, 37, 4, 13, 33, 56, 3]. The distributional
L56@P1: shift problem, wherein a cloned policy encounters unfamiliar states during autonomous execution,
L57@P1: has been identified as an issue in imitation learning [41, 9, 42, 43, 25, 19, 3]. This is closely tied
L58@P1: to the “feedback” problem in general machine learning systems that have direct or indirect access
L59@P1: to their own past states [47, 2]. For imitation learning, various solutions to this problem have been
L60@P1: proposed [9, 42, 43] that rely on iteratively querying an expert based on states encountered by some
L61@P1: intermediate cloned policy, to overcome distributional shift; DAgger [43] has come to be the most
L62@P1: widely used of these solutions.
L63@P1: We show evidence that the distributional shift problem in imitation learning is often due to causal
L64@P1: misidentification, as illustrated schematically in Fig 1. We propose to address this through targeted
L65@P1: interventions on the states to learn the true causal model to overcome distributional shift. As we
L66@P1: will show, these interventions can take the form of either environmental rewards with no additional
L67@P1: expert involvement, or of expert queries in cases where the expert is available for additional inputs. In
L68@P1: expert query mode, our approach may be directly compared to DAgger [43]: indeed, we show that we
L69@P1: successfully resolve causal misidentification using orders of magnitude fewer queries than DAgger.
L70@P1: We also compare against Bansal et al. [3]: to prevent imitators from copying past actions, they train
L71@P1: with dropout [53] on dimensions that might reveal past actions. While our approach seeks to find
L72@P1: the true causal graph in a mixture of graph-parameterized policies, dropout corresponds to directly
L73@P1: applying the mixture policy. In our experiments, our approach performs significantly better.
L74@P1: Causal inference. Causal inference is the general problem of deducing cause-effect relationships
L75@P1: among variables [52, 38, 40, 50, 10, 51]. “Causal discovery” approaches allow causal inference from
L76@P1: pre-recorded observations under constraints [54, 17, 29, 15, 30, 31, 26, 14, 34, 57]. Observational
L77@P1: causal inference is known to be impossible in general [38, 39]. We operate in the interventional
L78@P1: regime [55, 11, 49, 48] where a user may “experiment” to discover causal structures by assigning
L79@P1: values to some subset of the variables of interest and observing the effects on the rest of the system.
L80@P1: We propose a new interventional causal inference approach suited to imitation learning. While
L81@P1: ignoring causal structure is particularly problematic in imitation learning, ours is the first effort
L82@P1: directly addressing this, to our knowledge.

L162@P3: 3.2 Data Collection
L163@P3: To study the effect of dataset source, we collected data from three different sources – MachineGenerated, Proficient-Human, and Multi-Human (more details in Appendix B).
L164@P3: Machine-Generated (MG). We collected these datasets by first training a state-of-the-art RL algorithm [30] on the Lift and Can task, taking agent checkpoints that are saved regularly during
L165@P3: training, and collecting 300 rollout trajectories from each checkpoint. Consequently, these datasets
L166@P3: are comprised of mixtures of expert and suboptimal data, and resemble datasets from common offline
L167@P3: RL benchmarks [18, 19]. We excluded other tasks because they could not be solved by the RL
L168@P3: algorithm even with substantial tuning. See the appendix for more details.
L169@P3: Proficient-Human (PH) and Multi-Human (MH). Datasets are collected by humans through RoboTurk [15, 17], a remote teleoperation platform. The PH datasets consist of 200 demonstrations
L170@P3: collected by a single, experienced teleoperator, while the MH datasets consist of 300 demonstrations,
L171@P3: collected by 6 teleoperators of varying proficiency, each of which provided 50 demonstrations. The 6
L172@P3: teleoperators consisted of a “better” group of 2 experienced operators, an “okay” group of 2 adequate
L173@P3: operators, and a “worse” group of 2 inexperienced operators. These data subsets in the Multi-Human
L174@P3: data allowed us to investigate the ability of algorithms to deal with mixed quality human data.
L175@P3: Observation Modalities. To study the effect of observation modalities, we capture a diverse set of
L176@P3: sensor streams when collecting the dataset, including end-effector, gripper fingers, and joints, groundtruth object poses, and images from an external camera and wrist-mounted camera per robot arm (see
L177@P3: Appendix E). We have two observation spaces – “low-dim” and “image”. Both include end-effector
L178@P3: poses and gripper finger positions, and only differ in whether ground-truth object information is used
L179@P3: (low-dim) or whether that information is replaced by the available camera observations (image).
